column3: Description
Ayurveda is a traditional system of medicine and health care
which originated in the Indian subcontinent. The term
Ayurveda denotes “knowledge of life”. It is a compound of two
words, “ayu” (life) and “veda” (knowledge). The discipline
encompasses the physical, psychological, spiritual and social
dimensions of life, deals with dynamic concepts of well-being,
harmony, health promotion and longevity, and concerns itself
with healthy, beneficial and advantageous aspects of human
life as well as its unhealthy, deleterious and
disadvantageous aspects.
The coalescence of body, sense organs, mind and self that
dynamically supports, nourishes and propagates itself despite
its eventual disintegration. Ayurveda uses several terms as
synonyms for life, based on the different perspectives under
which they are understood:
1.   Coalescence of body, sense organs, mind, and self;
2.   Self-supporting, holding, ability of life to support and
preserve itself;
3.   Self-sustaining, self-nourishing, journey (of life),
duration (of life), ability of life to nourish and
sustain itself;
4.   Ever moving forward, life’s ability to resist premature
death and destruction through dynamic self-adaptation;
5.   Uninterrupted succession, sequence, consequence,
result, continuing link between past and future life.

beneficial.

generally detrimental.

The entire narrative of Ayurveda is woven coherently on the
logical framework of etiology (hetu), symptomatology (linga)
and therapeutics (aushadha).

A statement that negates the argument of the opponent.
A brief and incomplete or partial description of an
extensive subject.
A statement that clarifies the aims and objectives of a
proposed activity or action.
Repetition of a previously cited statement when it acquires
relevance in another context.
An arrangement of words and sentences structured and
ordered so as to make complete sense.
A statement in which some word(s) are lacking and have to
be correctly surmised and supplied to derive the exact
meaning of a sentence in its given context.
A statement that allows several discretionary options.

column1: 6  WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The narration of a topic in the correct logical sequence.
A statement whose meaning suggests the opposite of its
ostensible expression.
A statement which develops a subject matter in detail.
An indefinite statement which leaves its ultimate
conclusion in doubt.
A phrase or paragraph in which things with common
characteristics are grouped together and enumerated.
A statement specifying when and where an event occurred.
A technical terminology devised and used by only one school
of thought.
Extension or extrapolation of an argument or supportive
reasoning from a different context.
The word or part of a sentence which encapsulates the
actual meaning.
A conceptual construction, the work of the imagination.
Description used to denote a particular inclination, tendency,
or habit. Also refers to methods of diagnosis and treatment.
An exegetical commentary on, or explanation of,
Ayurvedic texts.
Description

column2: Terms of reference for scientific debates

column3: An established theory that has been critically examined and
accepted by qualified investigators. It may be common to all
schools of thought, scripture and branches of science
(sarvatantrasiddhantaḥ) or particular to any one of them
(pratitantrasiddhantaḥ).
A statement which aims to establish authoritative knowledge
based on affirmation or refutation of its evidence; in general
Sanskrit literature it means a debate/thesis/
proposition/ argument.
Technical rules for an argument or debate.
A statement which has exhausted the scope for further
questioning.
A question or query raised to challenge the expressive power
and scope of a statement and to clarify any ambiguity.
A statement which is beset with syntactical defects and
requires clarification.
Unconditional acceptance of different positions, including
those which are inconclusive.
A statement whose derived meaning allows for another
interpretation.
A statement that is not relevant or applicable to its context.
The response or reply to a challenge or objection.
Applying the logic of the proposed example to arrive at a
definite conclusion.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Arguing with the sole intention of finding fault with an
opponent’s statement.
A specious and verbose statement made with the sole
intention of unnerving the opponent.
A debate in which the speaker resorts to quibbling and
illegitimate commentary to argue their own case and refute
that of their opponent.
The desire to explore and investigate a particular topic out of
curiosity and with the intention of knowing the truth.
A discussion among experts in the field in the manner of a
peer-review.
A deduction or conclusive statement; the final step of
inference when affirming a proposed hypothesis.
Behaviour indicating that the opponent has reached the end
of their argument and can no longer defend the
stated viewpoint.
Correction of faults or defects revealed in a
previous statement.
A statement requiring proof; the first step in the logical or
inferential process of proving a hypothesis.
A shift from the original hypothesis, rejection of an initial
statement in response to an opponent’s views.
Offering a meaning or interpretation contrary to that of the
proposed hypothesis.
An enquiry or cross-examination based on
sequential questions.
Description
A statement deficient in any of the five components of a
sentence, thereby resulting in incomplete or distorted
expression of meaning.
A statement free of any syntactical deficiencies and
congruent with its exactly intended meaning.
A debate in which no counter-thesis is affirmed, and views
are refuted without objective examination.
Arriving at a clear and unambiguous decision.
Justifying a proposition based on sound reason, illustration
and conclusion.
Proposing a fallacious or irrelevant form of reasoning in a
given context.
Discussion and debate between peers which is conducted in
a friendly spirit and serves to advance knowledge.
The standard of examination which affirms valid knowledge.
Valid knowledge.
The tools which lead to accurate, true knowledge in Ayurveda
are direct perception, observation (pratyakṣsham), codified
knowledge, expert opinion (aptopadesha), inference based on
observations (anumana), reasoning, understanding causation
(yukti) and analogy (upamana).

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The immediate form of cognition arising from the interaction
of the five senses and objects in the world.
The process in which the object of cognitive organ(s)
(indriyartha),cognitive organ (indriya), mind (manas) and
soul (atma) acquire direct perception of an object.
Direct perception, observation without specific details of the
cognitive process.
Direct perception, observation with specific details of the
cognitive process.
The process of inference, in which a new conclusion is
reached from direct observation by applying reason.
A conclusion reached from stated premises.
An argument which appears to be fallacious.
A cause or reason; the immediate cause of an observable
event; the pivotal element in the inferential process.
A cause possessing all formal characteristics which allow
it to act as a sufficient reason for the inference of its
marked object; the independent variable influencing the
dependent variable.
Another term for the independent variable.
The effect or dependent variable influenced by the
independent variable.
Description
A fallacious inference which renders the entire inferential
process invalid.
The level of sensitivity between cause (hetu) and sign (linga).
When the sign is invariably present with the cause (when the
symptom is always seen associated with the pathological
condition), this is referred to as invariable concomitance or
sensitivity.
The level of specificity between cause (hetu) and sign (linga).
When the sign is coterminous with the cause and no other
entity (when the symptom is seen only with a particular
pathological condition) this is referred to as non-deviation or
specificity.
What is inseparable, inherent and essentially unified, e.g. an
organic body.
The chance effect by which a medicine appears to cure or
relieve the symptoms of a disease, when it is not possible to
confirm a clinical outcome is the result of a given
course of action.
The real and attributable effect of a medicine or treatment,
when it is possible to confirm that a clinical outcome is the
result of a given course of action.
Relating to or depending on special qualities, limited by
particular conditions, valid only under certain suppositions.
A type of inference in which perception is obtained by
negative concomitance (erroneous congruence between
two premises).
A type of inference in which perception is obtained by positive
concomitance (veridical congruence between two premises).

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
A method of speculative reasoning or debate.
Obtaining the proof of inference for oneself.
Obtaining the proof of inference for others.
Improper reasoning while making an inference in a particular
context; a fallacy of inference; one of the ahetu.
The process of drawing an inference based on an analogy.
The context in which a cause-and-effect relationship has not
been affirmed but is being examined or investigated.
Figuratively, an accommodating context or environment.
Figuratively, an adversarial context or environment.
A condition pertaining to the logical conditions of inference in
which minor terms uniformly exist in the same loci as
major terms.
A condition pertaining to the logical conditions of inference in
which minor terms do not exist in all loci with major terms.
A collective term used for deriving intended inference based
on five syllogistic steps, namely: proposition/declaration
(pratijna), means/reason or cause for obtaining knowledge
(hetu), example (drishtanta/audaharaṇa), comparison
between proposition and example (upanaya) and
establishment of the statement (nigamana).
Description
An illustration or example which can be understood by both
expert and lay person.
The agent which initiates action independently; also denoted
as cause (hetu) or doer (karma). It may be of three types:
inherent cause  (samavayikarana), non-inherent cause
(asamavayi-karaṇa) and efficient cause  (nimitta-karana).
Of the three types of cause (karana), inherent cause is the
most essential: it denotes the causal substrate or substance
in which an effect occurs (through inherence).
This type of cause includes only qualities (including relational
qualities) that inhere in the causal substrate and are causally
relevant to the effect, e.g. coloured threads in the appearance
of a piece of cloth.
This type of cause includes all other factors that are causally
relevant to the effect in question. A potter, along with his
wheel, rod and tools can be regarded as the “efficient” cause
of the effect, a pot. This resembles the cause of the same
name in Aristotelianism.
Statement of an authority or expert in a particular field.
The perception of the multiplicity of factors behind a
phenomenon or event.
A Sanskrit term which literally means “comparison”; the fourth
of the five means (pramaṇa) by which valid cognition of the
world is possible.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The objects of enquiry in any given discipline or field.
Etymologically “the meaning or referent of a word”, it is
applied to any entity that is knowable and nameable, i.e. an
object of experience.

column2: Six ontological categories of an object

column3: The object of experience is subdivided into six fundamental
categories: generality (samanyam), particularity (vishesham),
substance (dravyam), quality (gunaḥ), action (karma), and
inherence (samavayaḥ).
Denotes the universal or class-essence. The principle of
similarity may identify a commonality among different
substances, qualities and actions.
Substance is the substratum of qualities and actions and the
material cause of all composite things. This term denotes the
similarity between substances, e.g. flesh to replenish and
nourish muscle tissue.
Quality exists in substance. This term denotes the similarity in
quality exhibited by different substances, e.g.
semen and milk.
Action or physical movement which may lead to an increase
in a specific element. e.g. sleep increasing kapha.
Description
The unique individuality of the substances. An attribute that
causes depletion or decrease (hrasahetu), as well as diversity
and dissimilarity (pṛthaktva).
A substance which on consumption or usage may lead to a
decrease in a specific element or attribute in the
living system.
Qualities with opposing actions which result in one of them
being depleted, e.g. the pacification of vata  with usage of
sesame oil owing to its opposite qualities.
An activity which causes depletion or reduction, e.g. physical
exercise reducing kapha, which otherwise would increase
with inactivity.
Matter.
A group of nine elementary causal substances that underlie
the manifestation of all other substances, namely five basic
elements (space, air, fire, water and earth), self (atma), mind
(manas), time (kala) and direction (dik).
The five elements (panchamahabhuta) 1. Space (akasha);
2. air (vayu); 3. fire (tejas, agni); 4. water (jalam); and 5.
earth (prithvi).
Characterized by non-obstruction and responsible for the
space occupied by all substances. It is the substratum of
sound, perceived by the ears.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Responsible for movement, acts as the substratum of touch
perceived by skin.
Responsible for heat, acts as the substratum for form and
vision, perceived by the eyes.
Responsible for cohesion and fluidity, acts as the substratum
of taste, perceived by the tongue.
Responsible for mass and the force of attraction. It acts as
the substratum of smell, perceived by the nose.
Subtle physical state of all five elements from which a gross
element (mahabhuta) is produced.
Soul, the principle of life and sensation, the individual self, the
conscious element in the human body.
The soul in association with the living body, the vital principle
as the proximate cause of life and action.
The lifelong vital principle.
Perceiver of knowledge, soul.
A word which also denotes soul, but may be used figuratively
to denote author or physician.
The soul (atma) not actively participating in any action but
performing the duty of a witness.
Relating to the soul as the presiding entity over the body.
Description
The subtle body which consists of mind or psyche (manas),
sense organs (indriya) and soul (atma) and is devoid of gross
body; it is sometimes referred as the causal body or
subtle body.
The personal and animating principle in all sentient
beings, the soul.
Absolute autonomy, not subject to control by others.
The treatable entity (a person), consisting of five
elements and soul .
A body composed of 24 elements, namely: 1. eight primordial
entities (ashtaprakriti) including unmanifested microcosm
(avyakta), all-pervading intelligence (mahat) and the five
rudimentary, undifferentiated elements (tanmatra); and
2. sixteen derivatives (shodashavikriti) comprising the five
elements, the five organs of sense, five organs of
action, and mind.
Not experienced, unobserved, unknown, the invisible result of
works done in former states of embodied existence; unseen
consequences of an act.
Inactiveness of atma, indicating its principal quality of
performing the duty of being a witness to events.
Being everywhere, all pervading, an attribute of atma.
A process or state whose beginning cannot be ascertained.
Awareness, conscious self or intelligence.
Everlasting, interminable, constant.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
A quality of soul which is devoid of all bodily and
psychological ailments.
The ability to become irresistible, the condition of not being
subject to another’s will.
Not liable to change; imperishable , undecaying.
Synonym of the term atma.
Autonomy; an attribute of soul (atma).
Living beings with internal consciousness, i.e. their
consciousness is not externally manifested (plants).
Liberation, cessation from worldly existence or transmigration,
the fourth goal of life (puruṣartha).
State of self-realization of ultimate reality, which eliminates all
worldly miseries and leads to liberation and the emergence of
true knowledge in which the soul transcends the ego.
Attaining emancipation or salvation while still alive, liberation
from karmic rebirth.
A person with fatal prognostic signs.
Having died, after death, in the next world.
Description
The faculty through which cognitive organs (indriya) connect
with the soul (atman). Denotes consciousness.
Two features of mind (manas): minuteness (the smallest
possible structure) (anutva) and oneness or
singularity (ekatva).
Having the dimension of an atom , the smallest possible or
minute entity (cf. atomism).
Oneness or singularity (monism), in which no other entity can
supplant the role of mind or psyche (manas) in the body.
The rapid conjugation of mind with the sensory or
motor organs.
Not everlasting, transient, occasional, incidental.
Mind or psychic functions, namely: thought, analysis,
contemplation, mediation and volition.
The process of weighing up or considering the worth of an
action or its alternatives.
The application of reason in critical analysis.
The process of speculating about the possible or likely
occurrence of an event.
The act of meditating or contemplating a chosen object, a
form of focused thinking in which mind and body function as a
harmonious whole.
The process of assessing merits and demerits.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The characteristic features or attributes of the mind.
Understanding, intelligence or wisdom.
The controlling or stable intellect, the ability to restrain or
resolve impulsive behaviour.
The faculty of recollection, remembrance of things directly
perceived or heard (scriptures) which results from a particular
conjunction between soul and mind.
Six mental attributes or inner faults that lead to bondage of
the soul, namely: desire, anger, greed, delusion, arrogance
and jealousy.
Lust or desire for sensual pleasure; also, one of the four
goals of life (puruṣartha).
Also translated as fury, rage or wrath.
An excessive or insatiable desire to acquire an object
beyond need.
A state of confusion or perplexity that leads to incorrect
perception and error.
A state of being emotionally aroused, prideful and stubborn.
A state of being discontent with one’s state of affairs, being
envious, competitive.
A term for ego in the possessive or prideful sense; also, a
principle in the cosmic development of individuality or self-
consciousness.
A term that expresses self-command or self-control.
Description
A natural attachment, inclination or fondness for something;
often used as a synonym for faith or love.
A term that expresses modesty, sense of decency
or decorum.
A term that expresses proper conduct, decency, modesty
or mildness.
The ability to distinguish and classify things according to their
absolute properties.
A state of affliction caused by various determinants (vibhava)
such as the death of a loved person, loss of wealth or
personal misfortune.
A mental state characterized by infatuation or being
led astray.
A state of mind unaffected by greed, freedom from undue
desire, disinterestedness.
A condition of arrogance, haughtiness, insolence or conceit.
The four-tiered inner system: intellect (buddhi), mind (manas),
self-awareness (ahamkara) and the storehouse of moods and
memories (citta) which facilitate perception, cognition and
consciousness.
Time as a continuum, one of the nine elementary causal
substances (karanadravya).

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The points of the compass, cardinal and ordinal directions,
bearing points.
An entity that has not settled into any fixed shape or form,
and is not embodied.
A tangible or perceptible substance, or substance that has
settled into a fixed shape or form; also refers to material,
embodied or incarnate things.
An applicable or effective substance that is a manifestation of
the nine causal substances.
Any living, sentient, aware, feeling, animate being; any
substance imbued with life (including plants).
A division of the natural world which refers to living beings
which have internal awareness or inner sentience not
manifested externally, i.e. trees and plants.
A plant which does not bear visible flowers (apushpa) such as
the flowerless Ficus glomerata (uduṃbara) or Ficus
benghalensis (vaṭa).
A plant which bears visible flowers and fruits such as
Mangifera indica (amra) or  Syzyigium cumini (jambu).
A tree, e.g. Indian banyan (Ficus benghalensis L.) (vata).
A herb or shrub, e.g. country mallow (Sida cordifolia
L.) (bala).
Description
A twiner or climber, e.g. vidari (Pueraria tuberosa) or
kapikacchu (Mucuna prurita).
A small, nonclimbing plant, e.g. Abutilon indicum (atibala) or
Desmodium gangeticum (shaliparni).
A plant which perishes after bearing fruit or being harvested
such as annual herbs like paddy, pulses, wheat or maize.
Any living being in the animal kingdom which visibly reacts to
external stimuli.
An animal species which undergoes placental birth, e.g.
humans, lions, tigers, cows or goats.
An animal species which undergoes oviparous birth, e.g.
reptiles, birds or fish.
An insect species which thrives in a sweaty or humid
environment e.g. flies, mosquitos, ants or worms.
Smaller creatures which sprout from the earth or dwell
underneath mud, e.g. frogs.
A non-living, inanimate substance lacking all consciousness,
e.g. minerals.
An inorganic substance naturally occurring in the earth which
has a consistent and distinctive set of physical properties and
composition; a mineral.
Any artificial or synthesized substance.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Attribute, property or quality of a substance; it forms an
inseparable entity with substance (dravya); quality is devoid
of any action on its own, although it is responsible for action
through dravya.
The three primary attributes of the universe, also indicative of
mental attributes: tranquillity or harmony (sattva), agitation or
activity (rajas) and inertia (tamas). The interplay of these
gunas defines the character of a person or thing and
determines the progress of life.
Characterized by lightness, knowledge and enlightenment, it
is a stable state of mind and does not vitiate the same.
Characterized by activity, initiation, action and attachment, it
is capable of vitiating the mind.
Characterized by darkness, ignorance and laziness, it is
capable of vitiating the mind.
The five objects of sensory perception: touch, smell, sight,
taste and sound.
Trait of earth element.
Trait of water element.
Trait of fire element.
Trait of air element.
Trait of space element.
Description
The property of a substance which is related to body tissues;
it is extensively used for selecting and preparing Ayurveda
medicines and applying them successfully.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for
nourishment.
The quality of a substance which promotes lightness and
decreases physical bulk and heaviness.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for slow, mild
or low intensity activity or response .
The quality of a substance which is responsible for rapid,
strong or high intensity activity or response..
The quality of a substance which is responsible for promoting
coldness and stiffness (staṃbhana).
The quality of a substance which is responsible for promoting
sweating, softening or ripening (paka).
The quality of a substance which is responsible for imparting
smoothness, oiliness and moisture.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for dryness
and absorbs moisture.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for
smoothness.
The quality of a substance which is responsible
for roughness.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for density.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for fluidity.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The quality of a substance which is responsible for producing
softness or fragility.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for firmness
or hardness.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for
minuteness and consequent ability to pass through barriers.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for bulkiness
and consequent ability to fill spaces.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for
maintaining stability and position .
The quality of a substance which is responsible for
stimulation and mobility (preraṇa), and which governs normal
movements such as peristalsis.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for purging
and keeping tissues free of vitiated substances.
The quality of a substance which is responsible for providing
a coating effect to body tissues.

column2: Qualities of the soul or self

column3: The six attributes of the self (atma): intelligence (buddhi),
pleasure (sukha), sorrow (duḥkha), desire (iccha), aversion
(dvesha) and effort (prayatna).
The power of forming and retaining concepts and general
notions: intelligence, reason, intellect, discernment
or judgement.
Description
A favourable perception including happiness, delight, joy
and pleasure.
An unfavourable perception including unhappiness, sorrow
and grief; the opposite of pleasure.
The direct cause of action that seeks pleasure.
The opposite of desire. The Sanskrit term dvesha, also
denotes a suppressible urge.
The quality of being stimulated or striving to
achieve an object.
A group of ten clinical decision criteria commencing with
“paratva that support a practitioner in the analytical process
of deciding on appropriate interventions.
Priority, superiority or greater utility of a substance over the
other substances, e.g. in pharmaceutical preparations.
Inferiority of substance in relation to other substances.
The quality that enables determination of amounts and
calculations.
A combination or amalgam of two or more substances.
The quality of being able to divide or subdivide a
particular substance.
The quality by which one substance is differentiated or
separated from the other.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The quality by which the measurement of various substances
is possible.
The quality of being able to intelligently consider
circumstances and act on that basis; also considered as
one of the methods of investigation and examination.
The quality of being able to induce a change or
transformation in the original properties of any substance.
The quality of being able to repeat an action or procedure to
acquire expertise, as exemplified by the saying “practice makes
perfect”: an important quality for physicians and pharmacists.
Activity, one of the six ontological categories of an object. It
refers to pharmacological, nutritional and action in the context
of medical practice.
Coexistence or concomitance, an intimate and constant
relation between the whole and its parts or the basic
elements (mahabhuta) and their qualities.
Absence, negation or nonexistence: there are four kinds.
Antecedent nonbeing of an entity before its production or
manifestation.
An entity that ceases to exist after its destruction.
Description

column2: Absolute nonexistence   Absolute nonexistence, without beginning or end.

column3: Nonexistence of a substance in the form of another
substance. It refers to the difference of one thing from
another thing. e.g. a table is not the chair, denoting the
mutual exclusiveness of table and chair and the indepen-
dent existence of one with respect to the existence or
non-existence of the other.
The three principal texts of Ayurveda. Carakasamhita,
Sushrutasamhita and the writings of Vāgbhaṭa:
Ashtangasamgraha and Ashtangahridaya.
The supportive texts of Ayurveda. Madhavanidana,
Sharangadharasamhita and Bhavaprakāśa.
A glossary setting out synonyms, as well as the properties,
names and actions of drugs, plants, minerals or other
substances administered either as food or medicines to the
human body.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Ten important aspects of medical examination: principal agent
(karana); tool, instrument (karana); substratum of treatment
(karyayoni); treatment protocol (karya); immediate outcome,
primary endpoint (karyaphala); consequence, long-term effect
(anubandha); habitat (desha); time (kala); action (pravritti);
and ailment-countering stratagem, means of action (upaya).
The means by which an action is effectuated, the idea
expressed by instrumental cause: in the medical context may
often refer to the physician, who is instrumental in maintaining
fundamental bodily equilibrium.
The tool or instrument used for treatment, i.e. a medicine
or procedure.
The intimate cause of illness, i.e. a disturbance of the
fundamental bodily equilibrium.
The process undertaken to attain health or the fundamental
bodily equilibrium (dhatusamya), i.e. the treatment process.
The aim of treatment: to bring mind, intellect, the sense
organs and the body into equilibrium and attain a state of
healthiness or happiness.
Continuity of effect or long-term outcome, which includes the
achievement of healthy longevity.
Land, habitat or environment; it may designate body parts as
well as geographical regions.
Time in general including the seasons, the point when
something occurs (which may refer to diseases).
The onset of a treatment or therapeutic action.
Description
A word meaning excellence, goodness or skilfulness: it is
often applied to the physician and the justness of any chosen
therapy or means of action.
The ability to make correct and rapid decisions under
pressing conditions.
These four components or elements are: the physician
(vaidya, bhishak), materials for treatment (dravya), attendants
or paramedics (upasthata) and the patient (rogi).
The physician or medical practitioner is expected to have the
following qualities: to be an expert in medical treatment
(daksha), academically qualified (trirthashastrartha),
experienced (drishtakarma), in good physical and mental
health (shuci) and able to fully appreciate the state of health
or illness of the patient.
The material employed for treatment is expected to have the
following qualities: utility in various dosage forms
(bahukalpa), multitude of therapeutic qualities (bahuguna),
wholesome nature (sampanna) and applicable in various
contexts (yogyam).
An attendant or paramedic is expected to have the following
qualities: to be kind-hearted (anurakta), pure in mind,
thoughts and action (shuci), skilled (daksha) and intelligent
(buddhiman).
A patient is expected to have the following qualities: to be
able to afford treatment personally or through a system
support (adhya), consenting (bishagvashya), bear in mind
instructions personally or through a reminder system
(jnapakaḥ) and exert willpower (satvavan).

column1: 32 WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The regulatory functional factors of the body formed by the
synchronized interplay between the five basic elements within
any living system.
The three regulatory functional factors of the body are: vata,
pitta and kapha.
One of the three regulatory functional factors (dosha). The
functional balance governing all sensory perceptions, motor
activities and higher mental activities. The predominant basic
elements in vata are air and space.
Subtype of vata  seated in the head and controlling the
intellect, heart, sensory and motor organs and mind. It also
regulates activities such as respiration, spitting, sneezing,
belching and swallowing. Also denotes life or vitality, which is
evidenced by breathing and all kinds of movements relating to
the living body.
Subtype of vata seated in the chest region which extends
from the umbilical region to the neck or throat. Its functions
include effort, strength, governing the voice and speech
production.
Description
Subtype of vata seated in the cardiac region (hrdaya), which
circulates or diffuses through the body. It performs the
function of circulating of fluids through heart to all parts of the
body, as well as transporting various materials from one body
part to another.
Subtype of vata seated at the navel (between stomach and
intestines) and close to digestive fire: it is responsible for
metabolism and transformation.
Subtype of vata seated in the pelvic region and its vicinity. It
exerts a downward force. It controls functions like defecation,
micturition, parturition, menstruation and ejaculation.
Pitta is one of the three regulatory functional factors; it is
responsible for digestion and metabolism in the body. The
predominant basic elements in pitta are fire and water.

The seven fundamental structural components of the body,

nourishment and support to the body. They are primary
circulating nutrient fluid (rasa), blood (rakta), muscle

semen (sukra). The Sanskrit term dhatu also denotes group

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Signifies holding, carrying, preserving, protecting and

structural component in holding the body and thereby life
together and is also the specific function of bone, which
supports other fundamental structural components by
providing form and structure to the body.
The first of the seven fundamental structural components. Its
major function is nourishment. It is the primary product of
digestion and circulates constantly throughout the body from
the heart and nourishes other tissues .
The second of the seven fundamental structural components.
Its function is to give life. It is formed in the liver and spleen
with the help of colouring pitta and its metabolic component
and receives its name from the red colour .
One of the functions of blood is to give, quicken and vivify life.

The third of the seven fundamental structural components.

The fifth of the seven fundamental structural components.

predominantly of the basic elements earth and space. It refers
to bone tissue.

alleviation of disorder, normalcy of voice and complexion,
development of the body, increase in strength, desire for food,
proper and timely digestion of the food taken, timely sleep,
elimination of urine, faeces and semen and overall normalcy

Innate strength or immunity present since birth.
Strength or immunity attained by the application of rational

Strength attained by virtue of a favourable season or age, i.e.

Supportive structural component of primary circulating

Supportive structural component of blood
Supportive structural component of muscle.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
An individual’s inherent nature is the discrete phenotype of an
individual based on physical, psychological, physiological and
behavioural traits, independently of social, ethnic and
geographical variables.
It represents a person’s baseline state of optimal functioning
of both body and mind. The predominant expression of an
individual’s inherent nature in bodily functions is known as
body constitution with a predominance of dosha
(doshaprakṛti) and its expression in the domains of mental
and physical personality is called kaya/manasaprakriti.
However, for all practical purposes the doshaprakriti and kaya
of an individual need to be interpreted in consideration with
the following entities: ethnicity (jaati), familial inheritance,
genetics (kula), the influence of a specific geographical region
and climate (desha), as well as the ageing process (kala).
Body constitution with a predominance of dosha
(doshaprakriti) is a result of the baseline state of the doshas
of sperm (shukra) and ovum (shonita) at the time of
conception. Doshaprakriti is unique to each individual. It is
immutable and does not change during a lifespan.
Description
The characters of a vata-predominant person are greatly
influenced by its qualities: dryness, lightness, perpetually
moving, expanding, proliferating, quick, cold, roughness and
fragility. Accordingly, the person will have inherent
characteristics such as thinness, light weight and build, with
prominent tendons and veins; unstable/highly flexible joints;
rough hair, nails, teeth, face, hands and legs; fragile (easily
breaking/cracking/splitting) body structures (skin/bones/hair/
lips/heels); hypersensitivity to cold (shivering/stiffness),
intolerance of cold; with an unclear, unpleasant, feeble,
stammering, broken and hoarse voice; an unsteady gaze,
always restless body parts (eyebrows, jaws, lips, tongue,
head, shoulder and legs); a cracking sound from joints on
movement; sleeps less, and is easily awakened or stays
awake; talkative; quick to act (fast gait, eating, speech); has
swift and often hasty initiation of actions; is easily agitated,
intolerant, subordinated or frightened; is quick to comprehend
but less memory; and rapidly becomes fond as well as
disenchanted.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
The characters of a pitta predominant person are greatly
influenced by its qualities: hotness, sharpness, fluidity,
pungency, sourness and its characteristic fleshy smell.
Accordingly, the person will have inherent characteristics
such as a soft and supple body, presence of moles, reddish
tinge to facial skin; with pimples, freckles and marks; soft and
brown hair on the face, head and other parts of the body; with
lax muscles and flexible joints; intolerance of heat; strong
digestive power; excessive hunger and thirst; a higher intake
of food and drinks in quantity and frequency; sweat profusely;
greater than normal formation and passing of stool and urine;
a foul-smelling body odour especially at the axilla, scalp,
mouth and head; with less semen and sexual desire; show
the early appearance of wrinkles, premature greying and
baldness; and with a tendency for frequent ulceration
of the mouth.
The characters of a kapha predominant person are greatly
influenced by its qualities: oiliness, smoothness, softness,
density, firmness, heaviness, cold, slowness, stability,
viscousness and clarity. Accordingly, the person will have
inherent characteristics such as being well built and well
formed, with a firm, compact, heavy, steady and pleasant
body; with compact joints, and an oily, smooth and soft skin
without moles, freckles or dryness; a stable gait; with less
hunger and thirst; slow eating habits; an increased amount of
semen and sexual desire; slow in action and speech; soft
voiced; reduced sweating; with slow and often delayed
initiation of action; a cheerful and pleasant appearance, with
a calm and easy-going attitude.

vata and pitta.

psychophysical attributes of nature: tranquillity, harmony

difficult, it is possible that the specific mental and physical
personality type may be influenced and refined by education
and the inculcation of spiritual values.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
Arrived at through careful consideration of information and
the application of knowledge. Information is provided by the
patient’s narrative, the exploration of signs and symptoms
and the results of patient examination. The knowledge
derived from the learning and expertise of the physician is
applied to this information to arrive at a diagnosis
Ayurveda uses several terms as synonyms for diseases,
based on the different perspectives under which diseases are
understood:
Disease, a condition which causes various types of pain and
distress to the body and mind;
Origin of diseases from ama;
Illness due to multiple factors;
Illness as obtrusive to life;
Syndrome;
Fever as a generic term for disease;
Disorder, ailment;
Discomfort, disease;
A disease-state originating from the individual’s physical or
mental transgressions or demerits in present or past life.
Description
A disease that gives rise to another disease while continuing
to exist; it may also signify two or more diseases which
coexist owing to a similarity of etiology or
pathogenic mechanism.
The categorization of diseases based on various
established criteria.
Diseases which affect the psyche can be classified as either
agitative, reactive (rajasika)  or inertia-prone conditions
(tamasika).
A disorder of the psyche caused by an increase in agitative,
reactive tendency in the individual, e.g. excessive anger,
jealousy or impetuousness.
A disorder of the psyche caused by increase in the inertia-
prone tendency in the individual, e.g. grief, slothfulness or
excessive sleepiness.
A threefold classification of somatic diseases based on
vitiation of vata, pitta and kapha.
A disease caused by vitiation of pitta dosha in the body such
as dyspepsia, bleeding tendency or jaundice.
A disease caused by vitiation of kapha in the body such
as anorexia.
A disease caused by vitiation of vata in the body such as
arthritis, sciatica or paralysis.
A disease resulting from affliction of the psyche and body
including all psychosomatic diseases.
A disease resulting from morbid sperm or ovum including all
hereditary diseases.
Description
Hereditary conditions inherited through the maternal genetic
line due to morbidity of the ovum.
Hereditary conditions inherited through the paternal genetic
line due to morbidity of the sperm.
Conditions that occur at the time of birth which may be the
result of diet and lifestyle choices by the mother during
conception or from non-fulfilment of maternal cravings
during pregnancy.
Congenital disorders due to a deleterious diet during
conception and pregnancy.
Congenital clinical conditions resulting from non-fulfilment of
maternal cravings during pregnancy.
Diseases that manifest in the living system due to vitiation of
body humours such as fever and bleeding disorders.
Diseases and conditions which have their origin in the
gastroduodenal tract such as dyspepsia and vomiting.
Diseases and conditions which have their origin in the large
intestinal tract such as piles and constipation.
Diseases caused in the body due to exogenous or traumatic
causes such as accidental injuries and falls or resulting from
animal bites or poisons.
Diseases and conditions caused by trauma and injuries.
Description
Diseases and conditions caused by weapons or instruments
such as swords, surgical instruments, stones or wood.
Diseases and conditions caused by physical attack and bites
from both tame and wild animals; it includes injuries caused
by nails, horns, bites, snake poison and bee stings.
Diseases and conditions that arise from disturbances in
nature such as natural calamities, seasonal or climatic
variations, or following turbulent divine interventions such as
floods, epidemics or droughts.
Diseases and conditions that manifest in the body due to
abnormal climatic variations such as excessive rain, heat or
cold, and include conditions such as heatstroke or frost bite.
Diseases and conditions that manifest in the body due to
unexpected changes in climate.
Diseases and conditions resulting from poor adaptation to
the seasons.
Diseases, conditions and events that, in the absence of any
apparent cause are believed to be of supernatural origin: they
include those subsequent to natural calamities such as
floods, cyclones, thunder, epidemics and pandemics.
Diseases and conditions subsequent to natural disasters
such as thunder, lightning, asteroid impacts and meteor
showers on the terrestrial surface.
Description
Diseases and conditions that arise in individuals and are
transmitted by close contact with other persons affected by
diseases such as leprosy and conjunctivitis.
Diseases and conditions which manifest suddenly in the body
without any apparent cause.
Diseases and conditions brought about by the natural
progression of bodily processes such as hunger, thirst, sleep
and old age.
Diseases and conditions that manifest in the body due to the
natural effect of time and physiological changes such as
hunger and thirst as well as the ageing process, e.g. greying
of hair in old age.
Diseases and conditions that manifest in the body before their
natural time of occurrence owing to improper dietetics and
erratic lifestyles, e.g. premature ageing.
The classification of diseases based on their prognosis as
either curable or incurable.
Diseases and conditions with a good prognosis.
Easily curable diseases and conditions which have fewer
causative factors, lesser vitiation of dosha and develop in
body tissues which are comparatively less depleted.
Diseases and conditions that are curable with difficulty owing
to various factors such as multiple etiological factors,
depleted strength and functional imbalances.
Diseases which are incurable owing to the implication of all
dosha, multiple structural components and channels.
Description
Diseases which by their nature are not completely curable but
can be controlled or mitigated and symptoms palliated with
suitable medicines and dietetics, e.g. persistent diabetes
mellitus and bronchial asthma.
Diseases and conditions which cannot be successfully cured
despite the best available care.

column2: Tools for understanding disease and diagnosis

column3: The process of investigating a disease: it is conducted by
applying the five diagnostic principles
The fivefold factors that help in the understanding and
diagnosis of a disease, including its etiology, prodromal
symptoms, signs and symptoms, pathogenesis and
aggravating and relieving factors.
Etiology generally denotes understanding the causative
factor and expression of morbidity. Ayurveda uses several
terms as synonyms for etiology, based on the different
perspectives under which etiology is understood:
The factors directly or indirectly implicated
in the etiology of a disease;
Etiological factor;
Indicative factor;
Abode of the causative factor;
Agent;
Primary cause;
Causative setting, conducive factor;
Factors augmenting the pathology.
Twofold type of etiological factors based on discriminating the
etiological factor which directly causes a disease or condition
which acts as an additional factor in its manifestation.
Description
An etiological factor that acts as the direct cause in the
initiation of a disease by promoting the accumulation of the
respective dosha.
An etiological factor that sustains, aggravates and stimulates
progression of a disease or condition.
External causes that include vitiation of dosha through
alterations in food, behavioural patterns and time.
Internal factors such as dosha and affected structural
components  in the body which act as prime causes of
disease manifestation when they deviate from the normal
stage of equilibrium.
Causes leading to disturbances in the anatomy and
physiology of the body.
Causes leading to disturbances in the functions of the mind.
A classification of etiology into three types: these are
improper use of sense organs, intellectual error and
transformation under the effect of time.
One of the three primary causes of a disease owing to
misuse (underuse, overuse and abuse) of the senses.
One of the three primary causes of a disease owing to
behaviour based on erroneous judgement.
One of the three primary causes of a disease owing to the
transformative impact of the flow of time.
Seasonal variations leading to natural accumulation and
aggravation of the dosha.
Description
The normal physiological state of dosha underpinning a state
of equilibrium and bodily health.
A deviation of dosha from its normal physiological state of
equilibrium, involving a disorder of its functional, qualitative or
quantitative aspects: this is the basis of disease.
An independent disease or condition which has its own set of
symptoms and classical line of treatment.
A disease or condition which does not have an independent
existence or line of treatment.
A specific term which represents a pathological phenomenon
when vitiated vata dosha forcefully shifts another dosha from
its normal seat to another site and gives rise to symptoms.
Causes which aggravate dosha irrespective of the disease.
Factors that give rise to a disease or condition irrespective of
the dosha involved.
Factors which not only aggravate a particular dosha but also
give rise to a particular disease or condition; causes affecting
both mind and body.
There are four types of etiological factors: . proximate cause,
distant etiological factor, mild yet potential causative factor
and dominant causative factor
A cause from which a disease or condition results as a direct
and uninterrupted consequence, e.g. a dry or astringent diet
is the proximate cause  of fever due to the
predominance of vata.
Description
A distant or indirect causative factor which is less influential in
giving rise to a disease or condition.
A nondominant causative factor: it cannot independently give
rise to a disease or condition but may contribute to it when
the apposite situation arises in the body.
A dominant causative factor plays a preponderant role in
giving rise to a disease or condition: this kind of factor
produces instantaneous vitiation of the dosha, damaging the
tissues even before being processed in the body, and is
therefore very potent, e.g. a poison.
Recognition of the prodrome or set of premonitory, precursory
symptoms, treatment of which can forestall manifestation of
the disease; they are classified into two types depending on
their nature.
A classification of prodromal symptoms based on their
general and specific nature which may indicate a particular
disease or condition.
A specific symptom pertaining to a particular dosha. The term
also denotes those premonitory symptoms which indicate the
onset of a particular disease or clinical condition.
General premonitory symptoms. The term also denotes those
premonitory symptoms which may indicate the impending
disease or condition without providing any information about
dosha predominance.
Description
Ayurveda uses several terms as synonyms for signs and
symptoms, based on the different perspectives under which
they are understood:
Any morbid phenomenon or departure from the normal in
structure, function or sensation, as experienced by the patient
or observed by the physician and indicating a disease.
Morphological sign;
Characteristic feature;
Sign or mark;
Resemblance;
Figurative sign;
Clinical presentation.
Signs and symptoms of improvement signifying alleviation of
the disease or condition.
Different categories of alleviating factor used in the trial-and-
error method of diagnosis.
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are antagonistic to the etiology of the disease or condition.
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are antagonistic to the nature of the disease or
condition itself.
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are antagonistic to both the etiology and disease itself.
Description
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are similar to the etiology of the disease or condition, but
capable of providing relief.
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are known to aggravate the signs and symptoms of the
disease or condition temporarily but can provide relief from
the disease itself.
The judicious use of medicines, regimens and dietetics that
are similar to both the etiology and disease, but capable of
providing relief.
Signs and symptoms of aggravation signifying ineffective
intervention of diet and medicines.; one of the diagnostic tools
when a disease or condition cannot be interpreted merely by
its clinical features.
The sequence of events from etiology to manifestation of a
disease, which is classified into six stages .
Number of pathogenesis subtypes characteristic of a disease
or condition.
Pathogenesis subclassification based on the primary or
secondary ailment.
Pathogenesis subclassification based on various prognostic
aspects such as whether a disease or condition can be
classified as easily curable, incurable or difficult to cure.
Description
Pathogenesis subclassification based on which one or
fraction of the three dosha predominates.
Pathogenesis subclassification based on the strength of the
disease or condition.
A pathogenesis subclassification based on the time of
occurrence or aggravation of the disease or condition.
A factor, event or condition complicating a disease
or condition.
A harmful or prejudicial event occurring during a therapeutic
intervention.
An adverse event due to insufficient adherence to the
treatment regimen by the patient.
An adverse event due to an act of negligence or omission
specifically committed by the treating physician.
An adverse event due to an inappropriate or
inadequate treatment.
The presence of ominous signs and symptoms indicative of a
poor prognosis or impending death.
The different stages or phases of a disease or condition.

column2: WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda

column3: Description
A transient state of the body wherein the digestive, metabolic
processes come to a standstill and do not further transform to
end products, by-products or waste products. This standstill
leads to various changes in the body such as blockade of
channels, excess secretions, unusual accumulation of waste
materials, slowing down of movements and catabolic
processes. It presents with the following generic symptoms:
loss of strength, heaviness, laziness, tastelessness or altered
taste, and exhaustion even without physical or
mental exertion.
The ama phase is an initial stage of almost all disorders, e.g.
fever or diarrhoea, which arises due to vitiation of
endogenous factors: dosha, fundamental structural
components and excretory products.
Physiologically, the ama phase denotes early digestion of
food in the stomach.
An intermediary stage of active digestion and transformation
of ama leading to the next non-ama state. This can be a state
of natural disease progression or may have to be induced by
intervention to mitigate the pathology and treat the condition.
Physiologically it is the state of active digestion of food in the
intestines.
The transformative phase in the course of a disease or
wound indicating a post-inflammatory or
suppurative condition.
The state when ama  is converted either under the effect of
time or by therapeutic measures.
Description
A comprehensive term for the six prominent stages in disease
management indicating the stepwise progression of its
pathogenesis.
The first stage of disease manifestation, when dosha
increases in its own place or site.
The second stage of disease manifestation, when dosha
increases to reach the threshold at its own location. This term
may also indicate physiological aggravation of dosha.
The third stage of disease manifestation, when aggravated
dosha migrates outside its own location.
The fourth stage of disease manifestation, when aggravated
and migrant dosha lodges in a different location from its
original one and gives rise to prodromal symptoms.
The fifth stage of disease manifestation, when a disease or
condition becomes clinically manifest.
The sixth stage of disease manifestation kalah, when the
established disease or condition differentiates into subtypes
based on dosha and which may signal complications.
Examination of the patient by observation (darshana),
palpation (sparshana) and interview (prashna).

Examination of a patient based on analysis of information
acquired by the physician using his or her five senses and
by interview.

as breathing and heart; 6. tactile examination; 7. eyes and
eyesight; 8. build and appearance.
Tenfold clinical examination: 1. individual constitution;
2. morbidity; 3. excellence of structural components;
4. compactness of tissues or organs; 5. measurement
of body constituents; 6. homologation; 7. psychic condition;
8. power of food intake and digestion; 9. power of performing
exercise; 10. age.
A complete or partial obstruction in the body channels leading
to their malfunctioning.
A functional and/or structural alteration of the body channels
leading to a pathological process.
A structural and/or functional alteration of the body channels
due to vitiated dosha or ama.
The various types of the deformity affecting the
body channels.
Excessive activity with increase and overflow of contents in
the body channels.
Obstruction of the body channels with restriction of
movement; sometimes resulting in the formation of a
collateral pathway.
Description
Diversion to the flow of the contents and movement in the
wrong body channels.
Occurrence of a knot-like or nodular growth in the lumen of
the body channels.
Simultaneous or stagewise involvement of all three
aggravated dosha in the pathogenesis of a disease.
The simultaneous appearance of two or more illnesses.
The site of origin of the pathogenesis and/or manifestation of
a disease or condition.
A state in which vitiated dosha remains dormant (concealed)
in the body conduits. In this state, the dosha remains primed
to cause diseases when circumstances are favourable.
Aggravated dosha  which has migrated or been relocated
from its original site. Synonym: agantu-dosha.
Dosha residing in its own place.
A disease or condition due to coexistence of aggravated three
dosha , in which dosha dominance can be understood based
on symptoms.
A disease or condition due to coexistence of aggravated three
dosha , in which dosha dominance cannot be understood
based on symptoms.
Description
The state of being normal in every respect, without deviation
from or derangement of the normal state, function or quality.
Not typical, usual or regular; differing in any way from the
normal state, structure or condition.
When it is not physiological, the movement of dosha  within
the body is a pathogenic mechanism which results in the
manifestation of disease in different tracts.
Spread or migration of vitiated dosha.
Physiological or pathological movements of dosha towards
the structural components; diseases become manifest when
the vitiated dosha gets dislodged in structural components .
A movement of dosha towards the vital parts, including the
head and various junctures and junctions of the body.
Dosha associated with ama  undergoes qualitative and
functional alterations and becomes capable of giving rise
to diseases.
When ama associated with dosha undergoes depletion, the
resultant dosha is termed devoid of ama state; it is still in a
vitiated state and has not returned to normal state.
The inherent resisting power of the body, which strives to
arrest the occurrence, progress and re-occurrence
of diseases.
A natural, nonspecific type of immunity which defends the
body whenever any disease occurs for the first time.
The defence mechanism of the body which intervenes to
resist the occurrence or re-occurrence of diseases.
Description
A terminal disease or condition with no further treatment
options, other than palliative care.
The presence or co-existence of more than one disease or
condition at a given time.
A disease or condition in which the mind is first affected
followed by the body.
A group of diseases or conditions which are the unique
expression of a particular dosha  without the involvement of
any other dosha.
A disease or condition of generic etiology, i.e. due to
derangement of one or more dosha.
A primary disease or condition that serves as the etiology for
another disease and continues to exist in its original form.
A secondary or dependant disease or condition that resolves
when the primary disease or condition is treated.
An action taken based on an erroneous judgement, which
may be due to a failure of wisdom, intellect or memory
A forerunner or early symptom of a disease or condition.
A disease or condition caused by the combination
of two dosha.
A disease or condition in which the body is first affected
followed by the mind.
A disease or condition that requires, and which can be treated
and managed by surgical techniques.
Description
A disease entity of independent etiology and pathology which

column2: Three pillars to maintain health and longevity

column3: The three pillars are food, sleep and moderation in sensual
indulgence including sexual activity
Food is a substance taken to sustain life and is broadly
classified into liquids and solids. Liquids include water, milk,
oils, juices and honey; solid foods are classified into cereals,
legumes, meat, fruits, vegetables, spices and condiments.
The eight factors for selecting wholesome food are: nature of
the food item, processing, combination, amount, region,
season and age, rules for consumption and the person
consuming the food.
The six factors facilitating digestion and their attributes are:
1. heat which digests; 2.air which absorbs; 3. moisture which
loosens; 4. unctuousness which softens; 5. time which brings
sufficiency; and 6. balanced use of the eight factors for
selecting wholesome food in order to maintain equilibrium of
structural components and factors supporting the body (tissue).
A quarter-portion protocol in which an unwholesome substance
is gradually withdrawn from the diet-one quarter on the first
day, two quarters on the second day, three quarters on the third
day-and replaced with the same amount of a non-addictive
wholesome alternative. One quarter unwholesome plus three
quarters non-addictive wholesome substance should be
maintained on the fourth, fifth and sixth days. On the seventh
day the unwholesome substance should be completely
discarded and the wholesome substance continued thereafter.
This method is generally employed for de-addiction purposes.
Agreeable to nature or natural constitution; excellence or
abundance of suitable qualities: food that is fully compatible
with the individual and which is completely digested and
accepted by the body.
The consumption of wholesome and unwholesome foods at the
same time, e.g. intake of green gram (considered wholesome)
and black gram (considered unwholesome).
Food items that are antagonistic to the structural components;
food items which partially agitate dosha without eliminating it
and eventually become antagonistic to the structural
components.
Non-indulgence in sensual pleasures including sexual activity.
Appropriate indulgence in sensual pleasures including sexual
activity (in moderation).
Activities related to the body, senses, mind and speech.
A term covering activities related to diet, lifestyle, work and
recreation from the time an individual wakes up through to
sleep: it is prescribed in accordance with natural diurnal
rhythms and their impact on the human body and mind based
on the person’s age, place of habitation and seasonal cycle.
Routine pertaining to diet, daily activities and periodical cleansing
which is customized for each season of the year.
The transitional period between two seasons; it includes the
last week of the ending season and first week of the
beginning season. The regimen of the ending season has to
be discontinued gradually even as the regimen of the new
season is introduced gradually.
A cognitive and behavioural regimen to enhance well-being and
quality of life.
